(By The Associated Press) LONDON, May 25.—Britain, jarred into militancy from its centuries-old groove of ease and empire, called tonight upon its peace-born generation, boys of 18 to 19-2, to fill the gaps in home defense forces against the danger of invasion. The war office asked for volunteers from the age groups just under the conscription range after German bombs thumped on English soil over a 200-mile stretch of coast and while German guns echoed from just across the channel. Recruits gathered by tonight's call will have to enlist for the duration of the war in home defense battalions. When they reach the conscription age of 20, however, they will be transferred to training units for service in the field army, wherever it may be. Now it is fighting with the French and Belgians in Flanders. The volunteers for home defense battalions are distinct from the thousands who are enlisting

PARIS, May 25. (P)—The French fought desperately today to narrow further the 20-mile gap in the allied lines north of the Somme but blitzkrieg German units were still moving through the breach to the English Channel. French troops in the channel coast region, according to a military spokesman, were fighting off the German advance guards and were said to have checked the Nazi advance in the St. Omer region. Was 30 to 35 Miles. The Peronne-Bapaume breach yesterday was 30 to 35 miles wide but the dogged French, determined to save their comrades from the Nazi pincher movement, declared they had cut the distance to 20 miles. The military spokesman said fighting continued in the region of Abbeville on the Somme river 12 miles from the channel and at Boulogne, south of Calais. The whole front is "without change," he said. LONDON, May 26 (Sunday) (#) — German warplanes were believed to have dropped bombs off the southeast coast of England early this morning, but no damage was reported. In east Kent residents hurried into shelters and basements during an air raid alarm in effect for 105 minutes. British fighter planes were seen flying out to sea and antiaircraft guns were heard.

LONDON, May 25 ()—An Englishman who witnessed this week's fighting at Boulogne told tonight of being taken aboard a British destroyer while its guns thundered defiance to German troops swarming into the French city. The witness, Frederick Brinjes, a businessman, said the ancient, sunny city across the channel had become a shell-rocked, bomb-spattered trap for thousands of refugees. Brinjes, brought home to England aboard the destroyer, declared "no journey ever seemed so good to me." He told of spending two nights at the maritime station in Boulogne where thousands of hysterical men, women and children waited to get out of the city. They were without water. There were no sanitary facilities. Machine-gun bullets rattled in the streets. "There must have been killed," he said, "I don’t know how many. I know there were hundreds wounded and I saw many going mad." Brinjes reached Boulogne Wedn

DUBLIN, May 25 (UP).—Prime Minister Eamon de Valera warned tonight that Eire has been endangered by the fast-spreading European war and must be prepared to defend her liberty. De Valera spoke as Ireland was rocked by rumors of an imminent IRA uprising and sensational charges that a prominent young Society matron and others, some still unrevealed, plotted to aid a German parachute invasion. Every precaution was being taken both in Eire and Northern Ireland against a move by the Irish Republican Army or the Germans or both. Speaking at Galway tonight, de Valera said that the range of modern airplanes and the developments of the past few days had brought Ireland into the war zone. “If any military power considers that an advantage can be won by brushing aside the rights of the Irish people or their neutrality,” said de Valera, “it would not hesitate to do it.” Ireland has been endangered du

Berlin. —(UP) — Authorized military sources said tonight that swift German advances in Flanders had assured "annihilation" of the trapped allied armies of the north and that Nazi power would then strike with a "secret weapon" at England. Promising the most sensational military surprises in the blitzkrieg attack on the British Isles, it was asserted by Nazi sources that England would "find out soon enough" what is in store for her when the German offensive in north France has destroyed French, British and Belgian fighting forces estimated at a million men. Additional gains made since today’s high command communique announced attacks on the completely encircled allied forces have assured the destruction of these enemy elements, Nazi military sources said. Loudon. — (AP) — The British war office tonight

1940-03-20.text: LONDON, Mar. 20 (UP) — British reconnaissance pilots were reported today to have informed the air ministry that the Royal Air Force bombing attack on Sylt Island resulted in tremendous damage to one of Germany’s most important North Sea air bases. The pilots were understood to have reported that it was almost certain that little of the operational part of the base at Hornum on Sylt Island was left standing. The German hangars still were blazing when the reconnaissance and photography pilots swooped over Hornum at 9 a.m. and the barracks were a smoking ruin, it was said. The slipways were severely damaged, the British pilots reported. The raid was Britain’s answer to Germany's attack Saturday night on her naval base at Scapa Flow in which the British said only one battleship was slightly damaged. LONDON, March 20, (4?)-—-War Secretary Oliver Stanley bluntly replied to critics of Britain's war effort in the United States and other neutral countries by declaring to a Lincoln audience today that “we intend to fight in our own way and not in their way.” Stanley said that the foreign press had criticized Britain for a lack of enterprise and initiative. “This is a dangerous lesson for neutrals to teach,” he said, adding that “we are now learning that persons who ignore the rights of neutrals” receive their admiration. Stanley, addressing the National Defense Society, lashed out at those who call this, “in language culled from the ringside, a phoney war.” This is a phrase, said the war minister, used by people who, after a good dinner, sit down and urge two fighters to tear each other to pieces. His statement that “a nation which ignores the rights of neutrals” earns their admiration wa

Washington, Feb. 23 (UP)—Senate elder statesmen cautioned congress today against precipitate, retaliatory action against Great Britain for repeated seizures of American mail. Chairman Key Pittman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and Senator George W. Norris, independent, Nebraska, contended that Britain has a "perfect right" to examine mail destined for Germany. However, reports that British marines, with bayonets fixed to their rifles, had supervised the removal of mail from a clipper ship at Bermuda, aroused other senators to demand that clippers be prohibited from landing at British ports and that British ships be denied entrance to American ports "until the British have learned to behave themselves." Pittman confirmed that the State Department was engaged in "intense negotiations" with Britain over various mail inspection incidents and said he believed congress "ought not to

LONDON, March 19.—(/)— In a harsh metallic voice, beating his hand on the table in the deep well of the old house of commons, Prime Minister Chamberlain today used four words, “We intend to fight,” to stifle peace talk and dwarf opposition counter attack. To Hitler and Mussolini, he said in effect: “Whatever you have decided, we are ready to meet it.” In an hour-long statement, the 70-year-old leader of Britain at war pledged the empire to win “such a peace”—a “moral peace”—as was outlined by President Roosevelt last Saturday. His voice rose bitterly as he spoke of the Brenner meeting of “these gentlemen” (Hitler and Mussolini) yesterday, and he cried: “We are not likely to be diverted from the purpose for which we entered this war.” The somewhat cautious attacks of Labor Leader Clement A. LONDON, March 20. WUR—A sharp speech by War Secretary Oliver Stanley today foreshadowed a sterner British attitude towards neutrals in whose interests, he said, Britain is fighting. In the stiffest British attack on neutrals to date, Stanley warned that their attitude, critical of Britain, may induce her to follow Germany’s example and disregard their rights. By inference he reproached the United States, along with other neutrals, and warned that a defeat for Britain would mean a defeat for them also. The speech today followed an open vi by Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain in the House of Commons last night that British warships and airplanes would enter Scandinavian waters to attack any German warships which violated them. Chamberlain in effect warned neutrals that they should line up with the Allies and he rejected United States criticism of Allied policy with regard to Finland. “Pho

Berlin.—(AP)—D. N. B., the German news agency, tonight said three persons were injured slightly by bomb fragments in the British raids on Syit, but denied British radio reports that the airbase had been damaged or a munitions dump destroyed. The total accomplishment of the raids, said D. N. B., was destruction of an uninhabited house and three minor casualties. Fifteen to 20 planes, coming one at a time, or in small groups, participated in the attacks, the agency stated. It further quoted “British reports” to the effect that three British planes were lost.

LONDON, March 20—(Wednesday)—(AP)—A British air armada, hurling its might against the Nazis in perhaps the biggest raid in history on one fortified point, early today was dumping tons of bombs on the German island seaplane base of Sylt. The raid began last night at 8 p.m. (1 p.m. CST) and an air ministry communique said it was still in progress with the bombers flying in relays at 3 a.m. (8 p.m. CST), seven hours later. “By 3:30 a.m. (8:30 p.m. C.S.T.) all aircraft which were due back by that time had landed safely,” the report said. The first bombers, which led the wave upon wave of Royal Air Force fliers, already had returned, the ministry said, and reported the “accurate bombing of objectives.” “Some searchlight and anti-aircraft gun opposition was encountered,” the ministry said in its terse communique. The raid was Great Britain's answer to Germany's attack Saturday night on her nav

By The Associated Press BERLIN - Informed German sources today challenged the British announcement that last night's raid on the German island of Sylt was a big success but admitted that it lasted from 8 p.m. to 2:40 p.m. - DNB, the official German news agency, described the British announcements as "propaganda action aimed at erasing the prevailing impression that the German raids on Scapa Flow (last Saturday) made not only on neutral countries but also in Great Britain." The German high command announced that only a "house" was hit in the British raid. One British plane was said to have been shot down.

1940-09-09.text: BY EDWIN STOUT London, Sept. 17 (Tuesday) (/P) — Bombs hurled on central London by German warplanes early today killed a number of firemen who were atop high ladders battling a great blaze set by earlier raiders. Other bomb-set fires flared in a fashionable residential quarter. The pre-dawn raiders came back in thickening weather which had forced abandonment of their previous attack. Within a few minutes heavy bomb explosions were heard in the center of London and the anti-aircraft guns barked out their challenge. The fog of which British long have counted as an autumn ally had provided only a recess of less than two hours. Raid Called Off But after one hour and 35 minutes the Germans called it quits and the all-clear came at 5:24 a. m. rounding out the tenth night of air siege against the British capital. London, Sept. 7. (Monday) — German bombers striking at the vital heart of Britain’s Empire gouged hard at London today in the longest and most ferocious bombardment of the war — nine hours and 41 minutes of fire-streaked, bomb-blasting horror. The raid began at 7:58 p. m. Sunday, as night closed in, shrieked on with rising intensity through the dark hours, and finally ended at 5:39 a. m., as dawn drew on. All observers agreed that this furious onslaught was the worst in Britain’s history—worse even than the 8-hour and 18-minute raid of Saturday night and Sunday morning, which was disclosed today to have killed at least 400 persons and seriously wounded 1,400. Respite for Sleepless Flames from a new cluster of bombs shot heavenward in the heart of the city a few moments before the all-clear signal shrilled. Respite, however brief, had come to this sleepless capital. Just before the end, h

BERLIN, Sept. 9 (UP)—A German military source said that mass German air attacks on London would go on day after day and night after night until Great Britain’s resistance is smashed. The attacks of Saturday night and Sunday were by far the most severe thus far.

' LONDON, Sept. 9 —(U.P) — Germany hurled the third crushing air attack in as many days at London late today. The German raiders made dive-bombing attacks on some objectives and dropped “Molotov bread baskets” over thickly populated sections of the city. The bombers fled directly over the heart of London despite crashing antiaircraft fire that made the great buildings of the metropolis tremble. LONDON, Sept. 9 (4A) — Night notes in bomb-lit London: Going to work after an air raid starts, one dashes from shelter to shelter and tries to remember solid-looking places against which to flatten when the guns and bombs roar. A number of Associated Press staff men who thus ‘walked’ to work Sunday night, agree that the worst time is when searchlights criss-cross overhead, making an “X marks the spot” sign in the sky. Then, with a plane coming right above you, it’s high time to duck, and duck quickly. To one man who stood uncertain—“Well, are you going to come in or go home?” London buses continue to run after an alarm sounds, but when bombs begin to splatter in their immediate neighborhood they draw up to the curb and the passengers tumble into shelters. To the thousands huddled in shelters, the most comforting sound in the dead, breathless silence between bomb blasts is the click of in

LONDON—With the scars of front line warfare running right through their city of 8,600,000, Londoners counted a toll approaching 600 dead and 2,600 seriously injured after two nights of terrific bombing by Adolf Hitler's air force. At the same time, the defiant Royal Air Force made mass raids of its own against Germany’s great North Sea port of Hamburg, where tons of bombs were reported to have started great fires Sunday night, and Hitler's barge concentrations along the French coast. Given a day of calm after night-long bombings—up to 3 p.m. (9 a.m. E.S.T.) only a little anti-aircraft fire was heard when an unidentified plane flew at a great height—Londoners assessed the damage from the greatest raids yet carried out against the city. NEW YORK, Sept. 9 (UP)—The British Broadcasting Corporation reported today that one of the British fliers in last night's fight parachuted from his disabled plane, was machine-gunned by German fighters as he fell, but made a safe landing atop a barrage balloon. According to this report, picked up here by NBC, the airman was hauled to safety by the balloon’s ground crew. He was unhurt.

Air wars Biggest German bombers using new “super bombs” loosed on England in attempt to land knockout blow; London shaken by fierce bombardment, many fires set in longest raid of war. British RAF bombers strike back in three-hour attack on Hamburg; Berlin admits other RAF raids on Kiel naval base and Lüneburg. Mediterranean: British move thousands of fresh soldiers to Near East, reinforcing posts in Egypt and Palestine. Carol in exile: Abdicated King Carol of Rumania takes up second exile, reaching haven in Lugano, Switzerland, with Mme. Magda Lupescu; Gen. Ion Antonescu, Rumania’s new military dictator, freezes Carol’s vast personal holdings.

1940-10-28.text: By The Associated Press NEW YORK — Ambassador Joseph P. Kennedy, whose return from Great Britain aroused widespread speculation as to its purpose, announced today he would speak to the nation in a broadcast over C.B.S. tomorrow night. Kennedy, who conferred with President Roosevelt last night in Washington immediately after his return by clipper plane, and then declined to discuss the conference, said he would make no other statement today. His broadcast will be at 9 p.m. (Beckley time). Kennedy did not announce the subject of his address.

An Axis offensive struck at Greece today but met a quick counter move by Greek defense forces and Great Britain that brought reports of a naval action and British occupation of the island of Crete. Although neither Soviet Russia nor Turkey seemed likely to offer immediate aid to Greece, first reports from the Jugoslavian frontier town of Pec were that the Greek defense lines had held fast against the initial Italian blows. Italians were said to have made some progress, however, entering the Greek towns of Bibiho and Radoti after suffering severe losses. The Axis offensive in the Mediterranean began at dawn with Italian airplanes bombing airports and harbors in Greece including Athens; Italian warships operating to seize Corfu, and Italian troops, estimated up to 200,000, pushing across the mountains from Albania in the general direction of Salonika. London, Monday, Oct. 28.—(4%— Axis warplanes dropped tons of explosives and fire bombs in opening their sixth night attack on the capital last night but by midnight comparative calm had settled over the darkened capital. Millions remained underground but a few buses and taxis whirred through otherwise deserted streets. In one east Anglian town a raider swooped low to machine-gun a train but there were no casualties. Houses and buses also were splattered with machine-gun bullets. In another east Anglian town a policeman was killed and several persons injured when a delayed action bomb exploded. Kennedy conferred for nearly four hours with President Roosevelt tonight immediately following his return to London and announced that he would issue a statement to the press in New York tomorrow at noon. 1940-06-26.text: (By the Associated Press) LONDON, June 26—British landing parties actually have stabbed into the continental coastline front behind which Germany is preparing for the battle of Britain, it was reported today, and the sorties mark “a new phase of aggressive action.” Casualties were inflicted on German troops yesterday by naval and military raiders, it was announced, and some of the German dead fell into British hands along with “much useful information.” The clashes between the heavily armed British raiders, supported by the Royal Air Force, and their Nazi foemen appeared to herald a far-flung guerilla campaign to harass German coastal bases and obtain information on preparations for the invasion of Britain. London, June 26—British naval and military raiders, supported by royal air force squadrons, were reported today actually to have made landings on the German-occupied coast facing the British isles and to have clashed with Nazi troops. Apparently the sorties were aimed at disconcerting the German front and at obtaining first-hand information from the Germans on preparations for the assault on the British isles. “Landings were effected at a number of points and contact made with German troops,” the ministry of information said. “Casualties were inflicted and some enemy dead fell into our hands. Much useful information was obtained. Our forces suffered no casualties.” Prelude to Battle These thrusts into the German camp—the precise spots were not given—were made while British and German air forces clashed in the expanding struggle in the skies which is seen as a prelude to the actual battle

And now Japan slips into the picture of the European war in a big way, taking advantage of the wide-open situation growing out of Hitler’s attempt to dismember the British Empire. With France smashed and British influence in the Orient tremendously weakened by the Nazi holocaust, Nippon is undertaking wide-spread operations which patently are calculated to give her domination of the Far East and the self-sufficiency she has been seeking. This means a forceful reiteration of the “Monroe Doctrine” which Japan guardedly gave to the world in 1934—eastern Asia for the Asiatics. It involves control of great and rich territories belonging to Britain and the defeated nations of France and the Netherlands. In other words, Japan is speeding up her efforts to oust the western powers from the Far East and take over complete control herself. We may be on the verge of witnessing a tremendous increase

Great Britain struck back at Germany, with landing party raids on the enemy coast and intensified aerial bombing in a war that threatened vast new complications today. British land, sea and air forces cooperated in landing at various points on the German-held coast of Europe and attacked German troops, inflicting casualties, the British Ministry of Information announced. The sound was carried out while British planes unloaded tons of explosives on bases from which the Axis powers planned to launch their blitzkrieg on the British Isles. Germans Raid England Hitler sent German bombing planes against the British Isles, killing five persons and injuring nine, striking at air fields and airplane plants in the Midlands. British planes struck at the Italian coast and the big southern port of Naples, the Rome war communique said, but the planes were driven off, and planes also reported to have f

London, June 26.—(Wednesday.—(#)——-Two persons were believed killed in southeast Scotland early today during German air raids which extended over most of England, Scotland and Wales. British reported at least five of the invading planes were shot down in the Scottish attacks, during which large numbers of bombs were dropped. British fighter planes swarmed up to meet the bombers, dogfights were seen high over the English countryside, and anti-aircraft guns blazed away along the coast. The planes started before midnight, then kept coming, flight after flight, from southeastern England to far north in Scotland. Fires started by incendiary bombs were extinguished quickly. Explosions were heard in midland and southwestern England. Spectators in one town in southeastern Scotland saw a thrilling duel between a German bomber and a British fighter plane which roared up when searchlights picked ou

| WASHINGTON, June 26 (NU) Pe horaggri Roosevelt's advisory defense commission may place the cancelled Ford orders for thousands of Rolls Royce aircraft engines for this country and Great Britain with the Packard Motor company. administration sources said today, That disclosure came after William S. Knudsen, the commission’s production coordinator, had disclosed that the plans for the production of the engines by the Ford Motor company had fallen through because Henry Ford had refused to manufacture them for Britain as well as the United States. DETROIT. June 26—(UP) -- Henry Ford explained today that he had believed he was negotiating only with the U. S. government for a contract for 9,000 airplane engines, and that he would not build 6,000 of them for Great Britain.

HONG KONG, June 26 (UP) — Chinese reports said today that Japanese forces had occupied Mirs Bay — favored headquarters of Chinese pirates — and have thus encircled the British crown colony of Hong Kong. Hong Kong proper is on Victoria Island, off the south China coast, but its territory extends to the mainland Kowloon area, which Japanese troops on “maneuvers” have encircled. Thus, with Japanese forces in Mirs Bay, in the Kowloon area, north of the Portuguese colony of Macao and on the island of Hainan southwest of Hong Kong, the Japanese were in position to isolate Hong Kong if they so desired. Some observers feared the Japanese were engaged in a program against French or British interests in the Far East, perhaps both, and that moves at Hong Kong were designed to cut off the important British base from other vital bases such as Singapore.

WASHINGTON, D.C. -- WP — President Roosevelt's advisory defense commission sought another manufacturer today to build thousands of Rolls Royce airplane engines for this country and Great Britain after the collapse of negotiations with Henry Ford. William S. Knudsen, production coordinator of the commission, announced that plans for production of the motors by Ford had been cancelled because of Henry Ford's refusal to manufacture the motors for Great Britain as well as the United States. Ford has consistently held that he would manufacture "implements of war for this country only." Arrangements had been underway for Ford to manufacture 3,000 engines for this country and 6,000 for Great Britain. Knudsen said that the combined quantity was sufficient to justify the undertaking. 1940-05-05.text: LONDON, May 6 (UP) — Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain may save his cabinet in a House of Commons debate on Norway tomorrow by promising immediate and effective coordination of the fighting services it was reported today. Under the reported plan chiefs of staff of the navy, army and air force would conduct all coordination activities with Winston Churchill, first lord of the Admiralty and senior defense minister sitting as chairman and acting as spokesman for the cabinet when full cabinet authority was necessary to any decision. Despite vigorous criticism of the government in newspapers including conservative ones and by opposition leaders it was forecast that Chamberlain would take his cabinet safely through tomorrow's debate. Chamberlain and Churchill were expected to be the chief government spokesmen during the debate which is likely to continue through Thursday.

ROME, (#)—An attempted German invasion of England in the near future is not only possible but highly probable, in the opinion of Giovanni Ansaldo, editor of Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo Ciano’s newspaper Il Telegrafo, In his weekly broadcast to Italy’s armed forces, Ansaldo declared yesterday: “Everything causes one to presume that this war very soon will see a great effort on the part of Germany to invade England in force.” “Never were conditions in which the present war is being conducted more favorable to the attackers, never were technical resources available to the enemy on the continent so favorable. The blow planned by Napoleon certainly will be attempted again.”

Rome, May 4.—(4/)—Concentration of allied warships in the Mediterranean, with at least seven British and French battleships reported among the combined squadrons, tonight caused Italy to issue the bluntly-worded warning that she would repulse any offensive action.

(By the Associated Press) ~ PARIS—French report wide German attack on Saar sector thrown back in disorder; Reynaud government secret session test over Norway withdrawal in prospect, BERLIN—Nazis claim three-minute air attack sank 30,000-ton British battleship; declare total of nine British warships sunk or damaged during allied troop transfer off Norway. STOCKHOLM—German war machine’s expected push on Narvik where allies threaten isolated garrison; central Norway action finished. LONDON — Criticism of Chamberlain government mounts; critical commons due Tuesday; German air claims called “fantastic.” ROME—Italy warns allies any offensive will find her ready. SALONIKA—Greeks nervous as strong units of British fleet concentrate in Aegean, ALEXANDRIA—More allied fleet units arrive; Egypt orders general war exercises. LISBON—Government arrests 21 in move against “fifth column.”

México flatly rejected the "U. proposal" for arbitration of the expropriation dispute in a note made public by the state department tonight. In place of arbitration, Mexican Foreign Minister Eduardo Hay proposed that the Standard Oil and British-Shell groups resume direct negotiations looking towards a private settlement on the order of that to be announced by Mexico Monday, between itself and the Consolidated (Sinclair) interests. Trustworthy sources said the Sinclair settlement entails that concern’s acceptance of the legality of expropriation and payment by Mexico of $8,000,000 cash in three years, plus 20,000,000 barrels of oil in six years, at a price promising Sinclair a $7,000,000 profit. Law Is Cited A Standard Oil spokesman, in a commentary on the note, charged Mexico proposes to pay Sinclair in part with oil taken from seized properties and other than those of Sinclair. This, t

By KIRKE L. SIMPSON The factual picture resulting from less than four weeks of Allied-German fighting in Norway is grimly clear in an utter and stinging defeat for Franco-British arms; but it could prove a pyrrhic victory for Germany. The Allies went to save Norway from the clutch of the Nazi invader. They fled the field by order of the high command, under protection of the very Norwegians they sought to rescue but have apparently abandoned to their fate. It must cause sardonic amusement in Berlin that the first British soldier-hero of this war is the general who stage-managed the retreat from Trondheim with minimum losses. It could have been worse. That is about the best the British public opinion, newly steeled to (Continued on Page 3, Col. 8)

IN THE STEINEJER REGION, Norway, May 5 (Sunday). (®).— Thousands of starving war refugees descended upon the hilly regions around Namsos Friday and Saturday and helped themselves to large stores of food left by the British and French before the hasty Allied withdrawal. Upon learning that the Allies were gone these civilian victims of the war made a Roman holiday of it, eating and drinking as much as they could and then carting away as big a load as they could carry to their homes. It was a strange procession of vehicles of every description imaginable, stacked high with everything from bully beef to the equivalent of hard tack. Throughout the region from Overhalla west to Namsos—where the Allies kept their plentiful stores—there were poignant scenes as the hungry civilians clawed ravenously at the boxes of foodstuffs. Men, women and children, released from days of living in terror of air

BERLIN, May 4 --(INS)—Germany tonight officially pronounced her air force the master over the world's largest navy after triumphantly announcing a 34,000-ton British battleship was sunk by a single bomb and nine other war vessels destroyed or crippled with an estimated loss of at least 3,600 lives. The terrific mass air attack, biggest of its kind in history, sank a British heavy cruiser and a troop-crowded transport in the North Sea, off Norway, in addition to sinking the battleship, the German high command declared. Seven other ships were damaged and some put out of action, it was claimed. Distant Nazi officials acclaimed this history-making feat as the blow yet suffered by the Allies—a blow that crowned the German conquest of neutral Norway by turning the Allied withdrawal from Namsos into a major disaster. 1940-05-06.text: Linked Press Foreign News Editor, Germany claimed new aerial victories today over the British navy, but Adolf Hitler concentrated his chief efforts on intensifying the Nazi war of nerves against Great Britain. In the field of action, the German high command claimed that another British battleship had been heavily hit by German air bombs off Narvik, that a land munitions dump had been exploded, and that a British submarine had been captured by a destroyer. The British Admiralty announced that the 1,870-ton destroyer Afridi, with a normal complement of more than 200, had been sunk by German planes during the Allied withdrawal from the central Norwegian bases of Namsos, but British officials denied German claims of Saturday that a 30,000-ton battleship had been sunk. In Norway German troops swiftly mopped up the central front east and north of Trondheim and moved northward at such a rapid p

London, May 5 (Great Britain tonight officially denied Germany’s claim that Nazi warplanes had sunk a 30,000-ton British battleship and a heavy cruiser in concentrated air attacks off the Norwegian Coast. The Admiralty broke its silence of more than a day since Germany jubilantly announced that her aircraft had sunk or badly damaged nine British warships and transports off the Norwegian ports of Namsos and Narvik last Friday. “The German claim to have sunk a British battleship and a cruiser of the York class in the operations off Namsos

Berlin. -—(P)- British detachments cut off from the main expeditionary force when the allies abandoned the Norwegian port of Namsos have been spotted by scouts in a region north of Namsos, authorized sources reported today. The British were seen in the region between Mo, terminus of a railroad line and a highway extending northward from Namsos, and Bodø, a small Norwegian coastal town about 65 miles north of Mo. The first objective of German troops on their way to Narvik would be to mop up these detachments.

Sofia, Bulgaria, May 5.—(4)—Bulgarian officials said today that at least 50,000 Turkish soldiers are massed on the Turkish-Greek frontier in Europe. The officials said they were of the opinion the concentrations were “in accordance with British desires, and are connected with England's plans in the Mediterranean.” (Continued on Page 3)

(By The Associated Press.) LONDON—Clamor rises for sharper prosecution of the war; admiralty admits loss of destroyer Afridi, denies “Black Friday” sinking of a British battleship and cruiser by Nazi bombers, BERLIN—Hitler sends Alpine troops on difficult 200-mile mountain trek to aid besieged Nazis at Narvik: high command claims another British battleship hit by heavy bomb. BUDAPEST—Fear of war grips Balkans with German, Russian, Italian and Turkish troops on march and Allied fleet concentrated in eastern Mediterranean. STOCKHOLM—Northward movement of German aerial troop transports in Norway indicates new Nazi offensive to relieve Narvik. PARIS—Fighting surges around French outposts in Saar sector of western front for third day to rumble of artillery fire.

- Events appeared to be moving swiftly toward a crisis in southeastern Europe today, overshadowing developments in the north where German airmen, blasting at the Allies’ last foothold in Norway, reported they had bombed and damaged another British battleship off Narvik. Balkan capitals were keyed to high nervous tension as the sound of marching men and the echo of military preparations on all sides convinced them that Europe's great warring powers were gradually coming to grips on a new front. Turks Mass Troops Turkey, bound to the Allies by mutual assistance pacts, was reported massing troops along her frontier facing Greece and Bulgaria. Germany concentrated men and munitions near the Yugoslav and Hungarian frontiers, Russia bolstered to more than six divisions her troops facing Hungary on the north; Italy strengthened her forces along the Yugoslav border and in the Dodecanese islands.

BERLIN, May 6 (Monday) (4)— The German airforce yesterday attacked a British naval unit off Narvik, Norway's Arctic port, and scored a direct hit on an English battleship, reliable German sources asserted. Heavy smoke rising from the warship showed the effect of the bomb, British troops at Narvik also were subjected to the force of the German airmen, and bombs dropped on an enemy encampment in that region exploded a munitions dump. The German high command repeated its assertion that a British battleship and a heavy cruiser were sunk by German fliers Friday off Namsos, Authorized German sources last night stuck to that claim of success for their air force, despite flat denials by the British, Other sinkings included: A large British transport off Namsos Friday, two enemy merchantmen Saturday, and a Polish destroyer off Narvik Saturday.

By The Associated Press BERLIN—Remnants of Allied troops in Norway hastening northward for possible attack on Narvik, Germans report; Nazi mopping-up campaign proceeding. LONDON—Two members of fugitive Norwegian government reach Britain to confer in advance of Tuesday's expected brick-tossing session of Parliament; Admiralty denies a battleship and cruiser sunk by German bombers. PARIS—French command reports another heavy German attack on western front repulsed. OSLO—British bomb airport again; Norwegian prisoners to be kept in Norway. STOCKHOLM—Swedes, aware that war elsewhere would ease their tension, watch Mediterranean maneuvers keenly. BUDAPEST—Hungary announces smashing of big spy ring working for both France and Soviet Russia; Germans supplied tip. ALEXANDRIA—Backed by big Allied land and sea forces, Egypt ready for substantial maneuvers.

1940-02-24.text: BIRMINGHAM, ENG., FEB. 24. (AP) Prime Minister Chamberlain praised today Finland’s “heroic struggle” against what he called “a gigantic and unwieldy adversary—the Russian apprentice who has nothing to learn from the master in brutality.” Speaking in his home city in the last of a series of “pep talks” by British cabinet members, Chamberlain declared of Germany: “The German tyrants, not content with conquest, seek the extermination of people who resist the aggression.” Neutrals, he said, are fearful to maintain their neutrality before the “German bully.” He made a bristling reference to the Altmark case in which a British warship on February 16 freed captive merchant seamen from a German ship in Norwegian waters. Germany, said the Prime Minister, has sunk neutral ships without warning and helpless crews have drowned. However, he said a “neutral must not complain” if “Britain commits a mer

LONDON—(#)—Great Britain and her French ally, feinting cautiously at Germany in western Europe, were exhorted boldly Friday night by Leslie Hore-Belisha, ousted war minister, to make real war on Soviet Russia on land, air and sea—to save Finland and to shorten their own ordeal by fire. This revealing and vigorous speech was delivered by the forthright, unchastened Hore-Belisha to his parliamentary constituents at Davenport on a proud day for this island at war. King Attends Fete The greatest crowd since the coronation jammed London's old streets to acclaim the men who won the Rio Plata victory over the Admiral Graf Spee, while Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty, spoke with mingled exultation and sober warning of “this hard and novel war” at sea. King George himself came to Horseguards’ Parade to review and decorate the men of the cruisers Ajax and Exeter—and widows of the dea

LONDONDERRY, Northern Ireland—(#)—Bombs exploded in two movie theaters here shortly before midnight Friday night following an Irish Republican Army warning to discontinue the showing of British newsreels. No one was hurt.

Washington, Feb. 23 (4).— Senator Nye (R-ND) declared tonight that “arrogant Britain” would come quickly to terms regarding the seizure of mail if the United States would pass up Bermuda as an airmail stop. In an address prepared for the annual banquet of Grand Master Masons, he said: “If German or Russian or Japanese authorities were to rifie our mail as the British are doing in Bermuda, how easy it might be to enrage the people to an anger that was boundless. “Why not pass up Bermuda in our transportation? It would not be a week before arrogant Britain would come to terms.” Defended by Lothian After a half-hour conference with Secretary of State Hull today, the British ambassador, Lord Lothian, declared that the problems existing between the United States and England were “comparatively of small importance” when it was considered that “150 neutral ships have thus far been sunk by the G

New York, Feb. 23 (4)—The British and French purchasing commissions announced tonight that their governments had decided to place “extremely large additional orders” for aircraft and other products with American manufacturers. “The decision to place as much aircraft business in America as possible was, in large part, reached on the basis of the highly satisfactory reports that have been received on aircraft which has already been delivered,” said the commissions. “The commissions express the opinion that the business to be placed with American manufacturers may reach $1,000,000,000,” the announcement said. It added that “more than 75 per cent” of the orders were in the field of aviation.

London, Feb. 24.—(P)—A British release declared today that “it is authoritatively stated that no armed force of any kind” removed United States mail from a Pan-American flying boat at Bermuda January 18. The announcement was in line with an official statement issued at Bermuda yesterday asserting that a number of unarmed island constables merely created a “force majeure” situation against Captain Charles A. Lorber, commander of the transatlantic clipper, who had protested against removal of the mail for British censorship.

BY IFILL AQSVULALED PRED . . Russia’s relentless pressure on Finland’s strategic Karelian Isthmus followed its familiar, bloody pattern today as London and Paris, reporting on the other war against Nazi Germany, announced new successes against enemy submarines as an offset to the loss of a British naval trawler. While Moscow’s Red Army, handicapped by fog and snow, was reported advancing slowly but inexorably toward Viipuri, logical springboard for an offensive into Finland proper, the British press announced destruction of four Nazi undersea raiders. The Admiralty would not confirm this, but Paris military advices gave support by declaring two U-boats were sunk yesterday in the North Sea, apparently by British planes and apparently two of the four mentioned in London. On the debit side the Admiralty had to announce loss of the trawler Benvolio, 352 tons and the 30th British naval casual

LONDON, Feb. 24—(INS)— London had a brief, but apparently groundless flurry of excitement today over reports of a grave Russo-Turkish crisis. The anxiety was based upon a dispatch indicating that the Turkish Supreme Defense Council had declared a state of emergency, that huge forces of troops had been massed upon the Turkish frontier and that all communications between Ankara and the outside world had been mysteriously severed. Some hours later, however, Reuters News Agency announced that "searching inquiries" showed that the report of a state of emergency was "entirely unfounded," and it was assumed that corollary rumors of grave Russo-Turkish tension had been similarly exaggerated. (Editor's Note: Early in the day, Reuters itself had heard that Turkey had mobilized 500,000 men and lined up 350,000 of them on the frontier. This report was categorically denied by the semi-official Anatol

1940-03-12.text: LONDON, March 12. (AP) Exchange Telegraph (British news agency) reported today in a Stockholm dispatch that the Finnish delegation in Moscow had been authorized to sign a peace treaty. The dispatch quoted informed Stockholm sources as saying that the treaty would be signed tomorrow, the terms would be published then and at the same time hostilities would cease.

London, March 11.—(4)—Great Britain disclosed today, at a critical hour in Finland's peace negotiations with Russia, that she and France have offered “all available resources” to bolster the tired and hard-pressed columns of the Finnish army. The Allies, Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons, are prepared “to proceed immediately and jointly to the help of Finland” if the Finnish government should appeal to them for further aid. Chamberlain said that Britain had “not arrived yet” at war with Russia, and he refused to tell the House whether Britain was proposing to send troops to Finland and whether she was prepared to violate the neutrality of Norway and Sweden in doing so. (By United Press.) LONDON, March 12.—Authoritative sources reported today that a full agreement had been reached at Moscow between Finnish and Russian negotiators. Authorities that should know the nature of developments at Moscow said that the agreement between the Finns and Russians on terms for ending the war had been reached but not signed. They described the accord as “complete.” Allies Prepared. The report of successful agreement at Moscow followed a determined attempt by the British and French governments to emphasize their willingness to go to the aid of Finland and the unwillingness of Norway and Sweden to permit passage of allied troops across their territory. Both France and Britain also emphasized that Finland had not appealed to them directly for aid. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain had expressed the British viewpoint in a statement in the House of Commons yesterday that w

Paris, Mar. 12—France and Great Britain have organized and equipped an expeditionary force of 50,000 men for immediate dispatch to Finland if a new appeal for aid is received, Premier Édouard Daladier told the Chamber of Deputies today. Stressing the fact that the troops are standing by in readiness for instant departure, Daladier pointed out that they could not be sent to Finland, "unless a request is received." "Decision of this force has been made difficult by the fact that Sweden and Norway oppose it," the Premier said. "At a meeting on February 5th, the Allied Supreme Council decided to aid Finland with men. On February 26th, French troops were made ready, and departure concentrated at two points in France and Britain for their shipment to Finland." LONDON, (AP).— While Sumner Welles was hearing the views of opposition party leaders today Prime Minister Chamberlain reiterated publicly that the British peace aims are “freedom and security for ourselves and the small nations of Europe” and restoration of the “independence of the Poles and Czechs.” Chamberlain asked voters in a Leeds by-election to express “the national unity behind these aims” by supporting the house of commons candidacy of J. J. C. Henderson, a conservative party nominee. “We demand tangible proof that such pledges and assurances as are essential to the future peace and well-being of Europe will be fulfilled,” he wrote in a letter to Henderson. Welles, after breakfasting early in his Dorchester hotel suite and studying the latest news reports

London, March 11 (4)—United States Undersecretary of State Sumner Welles moved austerely through a day of social and diplomatic activity today in which he met King George, Prime Minister Chamberlain and other personages in his quest for information on the European situation. At 6 o'clock, after luncheon with the Duke and Duchess of Kent and tea with the King and Queen Elizabeth, President Roosevelt's fact finder went to No. 10 Downing street to talk with the Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax before dining with them and other cabinet ministers. The first of Welles’ formal talks with Lord Halifax took place this afternoon. He sped from the Foreign Office to Buckingham Palace and had a private talk with the King before tea.

British Broadcasting Company today broadcast a message from its Stockholm observer stating that an agreement had been reached between Finland and Russia although no treaty had been signed and terms of the peace were not made public. COPENHAGEN, March 12 (P). - Russian Finnish peace negotiations continued in Moscow today, their status screened behind conflicting rumors: After reports that the parleys had ended and the Finnish delegation was on its way home, the Finnish news agency announced that the talks were continuing. Advices reaching Copenhagen from Helsinki disclosed there were strong rumors in the Finnish capital that an armistice would be announced today. ON, March 12, A. P.)—War y Oliver Stanley told the House of Commons today that it was unwise and undesirable to attempt to predict what task the British might be called upon to fulfill in the future. He made his statement in response to the House regarding his secret budget for the army. It followed upon disclosure by official sources that several communications had been sent to Finland offering aid on an enlarged scale. "A token" budget was in keeping with the wartime arrangements under which Parliament votes on nominal estimates of £100 (about $400) by heads of the fighting services. Actual amounts—in hundreds of millions of pounds—are to be kept until the war is over. "We have a great army in process of formation," Stanley said, "and we are duty-bound to progressively take a bigger and bigger portion of the war on from the shoulders of our allies, the French, who in the early stages o

1940-01-10.text: London, Jan. 9 (4).—Prime Minister Chamberlain warned Great Britain’s people fervently today that they are approaching “a phase of this war much grimmer than anything we have seen yet,” but envisaged a reward for their sacrifices in a peacetime federation of European or world nations built upon British-French collaboration. As if timed to match his warning, Germany's warplanes swept down upon British coasts, attacking eleven ships, wounding at least 33 men with machine-gun fire and sinking a Danish vessel. Speaks At Luncheon The silvery-haired, 70-year old Prime Minister spoke at a Lord Mayor’s luncheon at Mansion House in the ancient “City of London.” It was the first of a series of “realization” speeches by which his altered government seeks to bring home to the people what they are up against in their conflict against what Chamberlain called “the powers of wickedness.” Chamberlain did

BY MIG ASSVEIGE Peo. A bitter outburst of sea-air warfare was disclosed early Wednesday to have sent at least six British and neutral ships to the bottom of the sea, including the 10,000-ton British liner Dunbar Castle, destroyed by a mine while she was carrying 198 persons, some of them women and children, toward the Cape of Good Hope. The dead and missing totaled at least 33. Nazi bombers invaded British coastal waters and sank one British steamer and two Danish vessels, the admiralty announced. Numerous others, including a fleet of five fishing smacks and a lightship tender, were raked with machine-gun fire. Of 40 men aboard the tender, 1 was killed and 32 wounded. The Dunbar Castle, owned by the Union Castle Mail Steamship company line, struck a mine off England's dangerous southeast coast. An undetermined number of her passengers and crew were injured, and two persons, at least, wer

London. —(UP) —The admiralty announced today that the British steamer Oak Grove, 1,985 tons, had been attacked from the air and that the number of casualties was not definitely known. Twenty-two members of the crew were landed. The Oak Grove was sunk. She brought to at least 15 the vessels attacked by German airplanes during the past 36 hours. The Oak Grove followed the sinking of the British steamer Gowrie, 689 tons. In addition, the Union Castle liner, Dunbar Castle, 10,002 tons, was sunk by a mine last night. The Danish ships Ivan Kondrup and Feddy, which previously had been reported sunk in renewed German air raids on shipping in British waters, still were afloat, the admiralty said. It was expected that they would be brought into a British port. Passengers Are Safe All 48 passengers of the Dunbar Castle, sunk by a mine off the south coast of England yesterday evening, were reported

'LONDON, (Wednesday). (#)—A terrific mine explosion last night ripped the 10,002-ton British passenger liner Dunbar Castle in two after Nazi warplanes, in an intense invasion of British coastal waters, had bombed or machine-gunned 11 British or neutral ships, sinking at least three. Two other ships, or six in all, were newly reported sunk in the last few days in the sharp burst of sea-air warfare. Loss of life totalled at least 34. Superb rescue work off the Southeast coast saved all the Dunbar Castle's 48 passengers and all but three of her 150 crewmen. The master and two seamen were killed. Passengers from the wrecked liner, owned by the Union Castle Mail steamship line and bound for the Cape of Good Hope from south of Africa with 198 men, women and children reached London early today, some of them wrapped in blankets. They told how they managed to get away from the ship in the darknes

BERLIN, Jan. 10 (U.R) — The Official News Agency reported today that three of nine British airplanes raiding Helgoland Bay had been shot down. The news agency said that no German planes were lost. LONDON, Jan. 10 (U.P) — The Admiralty announced today that the British steamer Oak Grove, 1985 tons, had been attacked from the air and that the number of casualties was not definitely known. Twenty-two members of the crew were landed.

PARIS, Jan. 10 — Several detachments of Canadian troops, the first to join the British expeditionary force, were reported to have arrived in France today. The commander of the Canadian expeditionary force, Maj. Gen. G. L. MeNaughton, and his staff landed in France last night from England, where Canadian troops have been undergoing training before moving to the continent. A full division has reached England. Britain's army in France already has been joined by detachments from India, the first overseas troops to reach France.

BERLIN--Germany reports eight British vessels sunk in raids yesterday. LONDON—Admiralty says only two ships sunk by Nazi raiders; some experts fear attack heralds blitzkrieg soon. COPENHAGEN—Breathing spell in Finnish-Russian conflict; heavy Russian concentrations reported on Karelian isthmus. BUDAPEST—Hungary works for at least temporary settlement of territorial claims on Rumania. PARIS—French report two German grenade attacks repulsed in Vosges mountains.

British airplanes blasted at German North Sea bases today and Nazi aircraft renewed an offensive against shipping off the coasts of England and Scotland—in the “grimmer” warfare predicted only a few days ago by British Premier Neville Chamberlain. Swarms of airplanes went into extremely heavy action over the German naval and air bases at Helgoland and the Island of Sylt during three British attacks, according to messages from Denmark, where it was indicated that an important engagement had taken place. Bombs dropped on Danish soil did some damage and Dutch anti-aircraft batteries also drove unidentified airplanes from the shores of Holland. The noise of planes, motors and guns during the current engagements was considerably heavier than on Dec 18, when the largest aerial battle of the war was fought when British planes raided Sylt and Helgoland. 1940-05-29.text: | By Associated Press | Fesecane May 28.—Britain’s air and sea power was poised tonight for a blow which she hopes will save the flower of her expeditionary force from the Nazi grip of death, clamped tighter by Belgian surrender and exposure of the Allies’ left wing in Flanders. Prime Minister Churchill, who warned the House of Commons gravely that “hard and heavy tidings” might be expected from a situation of “grievous peril,” kept to himself and his war council the plan for the break. But in promising a statement “when the result of the intense struggle now going on can be known and measured,” Churchill declared the trapped thousands would have “the powerful assistance of the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force.” Not Defeated Army Alfred Duff Cooper, British minister of information, told the nation tonight its army stood in great peril, that it would be necessary to withdraw the B.E.F. from

Berlin, May 28 (®)—Adolf Hitler’s German forces swallowed tonight the sixth nation to fall to Nazi arms since the war began and struck massive new blows through the westward rim of France toward Britain. King Leopold of Belgium gave up, ordering half a million men to cease fighting and about 700,000 Allied troops—already encircled in Belgium and Northwestern France—were thus left without any protection on what had been their long-held positions. The long noose-like lines, which the Germans had thrown about them were drawn tighter; Nazi forces were declared to have crossed the Scheldt Canal, northwest of Valenciennes, capturing the towns of Orchies and Douai, south of Lille, and advancing to the outskirts of the Belgian city of Bruges. On the Southern Front in the region of the Somme, the French were reported thrown back in "isolated attacks." The surrender ordered by Leopold opened at le

DUBLIN, May 29. — Ireland called up army reserves today and moved swiftly to put her forces on a war footing in the face of the grave situation confronting her neighbor, Britain. The procedure was strictly along normal lines. At the same time, volunteers began applying for service at the recruiting stations; but outwardly Dublin went on about its business pretty much as usual. Clerks, shopkeepers, laborers and others in the reserve corps reported at the Collins barracks and other designated depots for instructions. Volunteers to the defense corps — "The eyes and ears of national defense" — were augmented by hundreds of civilians eager to be Eire. The customary Wednesday half holiday was observed, however, in spite of general anxiety there was no apparent decrease in the size of the crowds at neighboring pleasure resorts and golf courses.

London, April 29—(U. P.)—The Allies have captured the Norwegian iron ore port of Narvik from German troops, seven weeks after its occupation in the German far northern blitzkrieg, the admiralty and war office said today, and authoritative British sources said the British expeditionary force trapped in Belgium and Northern France still was intact. The admiralty and war office, in addition to claiming the capture of Narvik from stubborn German forces which had been reinforced by parachutists and supported by the air force, said Fagernes and Forsneset, Norway, also had fallen to the Allies. Fagernes is on the shore of Narvik Harbor and Forsneset is on the iron ore railroad running eastward from Narvik to Sweden. Authoritative information that the B. E. F. was intact relieved anxiety which had increased yesterday when its vulnerability to attack followed the capitulation of Belgian forces un

Germany has failed to surround the allied Flanders armies. Indications point to successful retirements across the channel back to England, continuing for several days. It is now becoming apparent that the desperate fighting of the allies this week has been rear guard actions on a very large scale, covering the transportation of British troops returning to England. It may well be that a part of the Belgian army, too, was thus rescued before King Leopold’s capitulation. Germany announced the capture of Ostend only today. Dunkerque remains open to the allies as apparently does the strongly fortified port of Gravelines, between Dunkerque and Calais. Allied evacuations through these exits still may be successfully continuing. No Time To Reorganize General Weygand’s strategic plan from the beginning of the Flanders battle is now seen to have envisaged an eventual retirement from the Flanders p

With the British air force in diving, British bombers are hitting hard and often to ease the fierce German pressure on Allied troops fighting a way out of Flanders. German transport columns, tanks and armored convoy trucks were attacked repeatedly today with bombs and machine gun fire by planes which plunged as low as 500 feet over their targets.

Berlin, May 28—(UP)—The official German news agency D. N. B. claimed today that Allied agents have been concentrated in Mexico and near the Panama Canal to commit acts of sabotage which will be blamed on Germany. “The German government has reliable reports that an appreciable number of British undercover agents and secret intelligence service operatives have been concentrated in Mexico and particularly near the Panama Canal,” D. N. B. said. “The assignment of these agents consists in staging incidents and accomplishing sabotage which then will be blamed on Germany.”

LONDON, May 9.—British and French troops in Belgium and northern France (claimed by the Germans to be trapped and facing annihilation) are fighting stiff rear guard actions to cover orderly withdrawals, British sources said today. It was considered certain that equipment and materials which may have to be abandoned in the withdrawal from Flanders will be destroyed to prevent its falling into the hands of the enemy.

1940-04-30.text: LONDON, April 30—(?)—The British conceded setbacks today on the land, sea and diplomatic fronts. Military sources said the Germans had captured Storen, a railroad junction 30 miles south of Nazi-held Trondheim, which may prove to be the key to the whole campaign in Norway. The admiralty announced that two submarines were overdue and must be regarded as lost. They are the 1,095-ton Tarpon, which carried a normal crew of 53, and the 678-ton Sterlet whose normal complement was 40. This raised Britain's loss of undersea craft to seven of the 57 with which she entered the war last September and the known loss of life to 188. The admiralty also disclosed the sinking of the 452-ton trawler Bradman and the 590-ton trawler Cape Sirctoko, but said there was no loss of life in either case. As trade talks with Russia struck a snag over Russian exports to Germany, Ronald H. Cross, minister directing

STOCKHOLM, April 30. (7) — German troops in arctic Narvik, their artillery smashed, were reported today to be clinging to shoreline machine gun nests under heavy bombardment from British naval forces. Advices from Rikszransen, Swedish border station on the iron ore line from Narvik, said that the Germans had lost all of their mountain artillery positions and that a German battery in a Narvik churchyard had been destroyed by the British guns. A mortuary chapel also was smashed.

LONDON, MAY 1. (AP).—The War Office announced today that British troops "withdrew to prepared positions" in the important Dombas area, 100 miles south of Trondheim, after stubbornly resisting strong German attacks. The communique, issued after a military spokesman had described the position of British forces in Central Norway as "dangerous and very obscure," said: "At Narvik (Arctic ore port) areas occupied by Allied forces have been extended and operations are continuing satisfactorily. "In the Namsos area (Central Norway north of Trondheim) the situation at the front remains unchanged. "In the Dombas area our troops, after stubborn resistance in the face of strong enemy attacks, withdrew to prepared positions." Efforts to relieve the Allied forces continued while the British air force struck savagely at three German air bases in Scandinavia. Allied anxiety lest German successes in Norw

LONDON, April 30 (U.P)—A British military spokesman reported today that the Germans had taken the key town of Stoeren in Norway, 25 miles south of the great German base at Trondheim, and admitted the situation of allied troops in the Dombaas-Stoeren area was difficult. Confirmation of the report would mean that the Germans, driving up the two main valleys from southern Norway, were within 25 miles of their goal—juncture of forces with the Germans holding Trondheim. However, an hour after the military spokesman had reported the German occupation of Stoeren, the ministry of information said: “The report Stoeren is in German hands is a rumor emanating from Swedish forces which is not confirmed.” Nazi Forces Advance It was indicated German motorized forces were driving strongly up the Gudbrands valley, that they had taken the town of Otta where the allies had made a stand, and they were now

London, April 29.—(#)— Damaging attacks by low-flying German bombers on the Allied troop landing bases of Molde and Andalsnes emphasized in British minds tonight the belief that control of the air will be the decisive factor in the major battle slowly developing in central Norway. Aware that German planes also are harrying British lines of communication and protecting the German columns moving swiftly from the south toward the garrison in Trondheim, London was gloomy after a week of indifferent news from the north. Meanwhile, however, Britain appeared determined to plug any possible gaps on the diplomatic and economic fronts. FORMOFOSS, Norway (About 20 miles east of Namsos) April 30—'45— German air raids on the Allied troops at Namsos, which have turned parts of that Norwegian coastal town into wreckage, took a sharp decline yesterday when British anti-aircraft guns opened up full blast and drove a surprised German bomber high into the upper air. After that blast the air alarms which have kept the entire Namsos area anxious since the first days of Germany's invasion of Norway lessened by 80 percent. Namsos, which has steep rising cliffs on the north side, a fjord in the center and more hills on the south, now is literally alive with British and French anti-aircraft batteries. Each is manned by crack shots especially chosen to bolster the morale of the Norwegians, who have clung to their homes in this embattled town. German fliers, who, according to Norwegian airmen, formerly flew over the entire sector from

LONDON, WO—British ships were ordered Tuesday night to take the Cape of Good Hope route around Africa to the far east and keep out of the Mediterranean because of the attitude of Italian leaders toward the European war. The action was taken because of Italy's threatening attitude toward the allied powers, it was stated authoritatively, but hope was expressed that circumstances in the near future would permit abandonment of the shipping precautions. Britain and France recently have made overtures to Italy for a settlement of Italy's grievances, but without result. Fascist leaders have warned that Italy could not stay outside the war and the press has declared the fascists would fight only on the side of Germany. The importance of the British action was emphasized by the fact that the Mediterranean route—described as the ‘lifeline of the British empire—was not closed to British shipping ev

LONDON, April 30 — (UP) — The German people as well as the Nazi leaders are responsible for the prolongation of Europe's war, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the House of Commons today. Chamberlain, who previously had dodged questions regarding progress of the war in Norway, was questioned in the light of a recent speech by Alfred Duff Cooper, former First Lord of the Admiralty, who said that the Allies must “defeat in battle” the German people as well as the Nazi leaders. The speech was criticized by some British newspapers on the grounds that it made difficult the possibility of a stable future peace in Europe. “In my speech at Mansion House on Jan. 8,” Chamberlain said, “I pointed out that the Allies have no vindictive designs against the German people but that, on the other hand, the German people must realize the responsibility for

1940-02-10.text: London, Feb. 9 (4).—Great Britain’s Admiralty in a terse but prideful communique tonight announced that a single destroyer of His Majesty’s Navy had sunk two German submarines while they were attacking a convoy. Disclosure of this double blow to Nazi undersea strength came at the end of a day in which British and neutral coastal shipping felt the fury of German aerial bombs in the fourth series of attacks in twelve days. One German plane was shot down by British fighting planes, two others damaged and still more scattered out to sea. At Least 40 Sunk The destruction of the U-boats today brought to at least 40 the unofficial estimate of Germany's total submarine losses, or probably one-

Cautious restraint today greeted President Roosevelt's decision to send Sumner Welles, United States undersecretary of state, to Europe to investigate “present conditions.” Welles was assured a cordial reception at Rome, his first step, but there as in London, Berlin and Paris his forthcoming visit was regarded primarily as a quest for information despite its link in the United States with American steps toward “eventual restoration of world peace.” Informed fascists said it was natural the Italian attitude should be reserved since the aims of the mission so far were “rather vague.”

TOENDER, Denmark, /)—A British bomber raided the German naval base on the Island of Sylt Saturday, Danish observers said, dropping four bombs. Observers at the Danish frontier said they saw the plane pass over the southern part of the island then wheel westward toward the sea after unloading the bombs. Six German fighters pursued the British plane but the bomber appeared to have escaped.

LONDON, Feb. 10—Torpedoing of the Canadian Pacific freighter Beaverburn was a victory that apparently cost Germany two submarines. The admiralty announced late last night a single British destroyer had sunk two U-boats as they attempted to attack a convoy. The announcement followed statements attributed to an officer of the destroyer, which escorted a rescue ship to a west English port with survivors of the 9,874-ton Beaverburn, sunk off southern Ireland, apparently Monday. The admiralty did not say when or where the fight occurred or identify the destroyer. It was disclosed, however, the 5,406-ton Scottish steamer Chagres, another member of the convoy, later was sunk by a mine. The report brought total German submarine losses to an unofficial total of at least 40, half or more of the number believed in operation at the start of the war.

LONDON—Skepticism in big European capitals and vague hope in small neutral ones greeted President Roosevelt's peace initiative today. Special Envoy Sumner Welles was assured a cordial welcome wherever he might go on his mission to investigate and report to the President on present conditions in Europe, and interest was shown in the disclosure that Secretary of State Cordell Hull already was in communication with neutral nations which have been working for peace. But the emphasis of belligerents for the moment was put on the prosecution of the war: neutrals were concerned by the danger that other nations would be dragged into it. The situations in Scandinavia, the Balkans and the Near East were regarded as most delicate. It was at once noted that though Welles was going to Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy he was not going to Russia, the fifth great European power. There was specul

Berlin, Feb. 10 The German high command reported today that British bombers made an unsuccessful attempt to penetrate Helgoland bight, and affirmed DNB news agency reports that eight ships had been sunk or wrecked by German air raiders yesterday; with one German plane lost. A communique said: "As already reported, six British ships or ships in British convoys, with a total tonnage of about 15,000, and two British patrol boats were sunk or so seriously damaged that they must be regarded as a total loss, by German air units which made armed patrols over the North Sea." "Despite heavy anti-aircraft fire and defense by pursuit planes, only one German plane is missing. "Yesterday afternoon a number of British planes tried to penetrate the German (Helgoland) bight. They achieved no success and were driven off by our defense forces."

Associated Press Staff Writer. There is obviously a suspicion in Berlin, as well as in London and Paris, that Soviet Russia may move in the spring to upset the status quo in southeastern Europe. It seems equally clear that the Reich is virtually as anxious as the allies to prevent that from happening. The Nazis want no trouble of any kind that might disrupt their supply lines in that quarter of the world. This is shown by their calm reaction to recent developments in Turkey. Despite virtual Turkish expropriation of an important German-owned shipyard in the Dardanelles area, and a simultaneous purge of German technical experts from Turkish national defense payrolls, Berlin sees no probability of a serious diplomatic tangle with Turkey. A day when Germany and her Franco-British foes actually could follow the recent advice of former Kaiser Wilhelm and drop their own war to join forces again

BRISTOL, England, Feb. 19. (4)—Sir Kingsley Wood asserted today the Russo-German pact was both a political and material disappointment to the Reich, and attacked as “abominable” conditions in German-occupied Poland. The air minister, in the sixth of a series of ministerial speeches said terms of the pact were “unknown outside the Kremlin and the inner circles of the Nazi party,” but that it was “uncertain and doubtful bargain,” and the “compelling cause of uneasiness in Germany.” TRANSPORT DIFFICULTIES He said Russian transport difficulties must have greatly damaged any hope there may have been of Germany obtaining adequate supplies of oil and raw materials from Russia. Citing an assertion by the Polish government-in-exile that 15,000 persons had been shot in German-occupied Poland, Sir Kingsley declared conditions there were far worse than Russian-occupied Poland. “German methods in occ

1940-12-28.text: BUDAPEST, Dec. 28. (®) — With the advance guard of a new Nazi expedition of 300,000 troops already rolling eastward across Hungary, authoritative sources reported today that Germany plans to move against Greece by way of Bulgaria only if Britain tries to use Greece as the starting point for an invasion of central Europe. Germany, these sources said, will not make any move to aid the Italian forces now fighting the Greeks in Albania if the British refrain from landing troops in Greece. Germany was understood by these sources to have let it be known in the Balkans that in the event of Italian collapse as the result of a Greek victory the Nazis would hasten to make a definite peace with France. It was stated authoritatively that Adolf Hitler had agreed to let Premier Mussolini attack Greece last October only because he wished to divert Italy's attention from beaten France. Germany was said

Washington, Dec. 28 (f)—Further opposition to President Roosevelt's “lend-lease” plan of furnishing war supplies to Great Britain developed today, with Senator Wheeler (D-Mont) announcing that he would broadcast his objections to the proposal Monday night. The speech, to be carried at 9:40 p.m. (Emporia time) over a national hookup will be rebroadcast to foreign countries by short wave. Wheeler, who this week urged the administration to “force peace on Europe,” said he would discuss foreign affairs generally and the “lend-lease” proposal specifically. He also was expected to comment on the President’s national radio address to be delivered Sunday night.

Virginio Gayda, authoritative Italian commentator, asserted that this would violate U. S. neutrality and warned that any flagrant violation of neutrality by the United States would bring Japan into the war under the terms of the Berlin-Rome-Tokyo military alliance. SHOULDER TO SHOULDER An authorized Nazi spokesman made plain that the Axis partners stood shoulder to shoulder in the new propaganda attack, asserting that similar German press comment "clearly discussed the situation in the correct proportions." MELBOURNE, Australia, Dec. 23 —The sea raider which bombed the British-mandated island Nauru yesterday ran down the Japanese flag and hoisted the Nazi swastika before opening fire, the navy ministry announced today. Navy Minister William M. Hughes, who made the announcement, said the raider appeared before dawn off the 6,400-acre Guano island, in the equatorial Pacific, and signaled with its Morse lamp: “Do not use wireless or I will shoot mast down. I am going to shoot at stores and phosphate jetties.” Hughes said the instructions were obeyed and the radio station was left intact. The raider fired on loading equipment, stores and fuel tanks, but left private houses untouched.

BERLIN, Dec. 28. — (U.P.) — Authorized quarters backed up and endorsed German newspaper warnings to the United States today against attempting to send supplies to Great Britain via Ireland in American ships. An inspired press editorial campaign had warned that if United States ships sailed in or out of convoy to Ireland they were liable to be sunk. “I think the way the German press handled this Irish problem was excellent and it clearly discussed the situation in correct proportions,” a spokesman for authorized quarters said. An earlier spokesman had refused to comment on the German newspaper editorials, intimating that they would make public statements only if any such American plan were mentioned by official or semi-official sources at Washington.

LONDON, Dec. 28.—(Saturday)—The German air force delivered a short but furious blow at London last night which left no doubt that the tacit Christmas truce in this bitter air war is now only history. For some hours flares, then incendiaries and finally heavy bombs fell in district after district. The "raiders passed" signal sounded an hour before midnight, but in the preceding hours, British sources said, the raid was equal in intensity to some of the heaviest attacks on London. It was the first sign of bombing London had seen after three strangely quiet nights. There were casualties—it is not permitted to say how many. Some persons were killed and injured when a public shelter was hit. One woman, pinned under a gas stove with fire burning around her, joked for two hours with the rescue squad that finally got her out. She died a few minutes later. RO Fee Avo eee eee BERLIN, Dec. 28—The sinking of four armed British merchant ships totalling 24,340 tons, and a fifth ship of 12,823 tons, identified as the "Waiotira", was officially credited by the high command to two German submarines. Also, a German scouting plane was credited with dumping two heavy bombs on 4 merchant ships of 9,000 to 10,000 tons yesterday east of the Thames mouth. Informed sources said the vessel burst into flames and presumably sank. A "few" British planes penetrated a German-held coastal region during the night, the high command reported, but it said no bombs were dropped on German territory. German warplanes were reported to have bombed London during the night with fire-bombs and high explosives. Returning pilots were quoted as saying they left numerous fires burning.

LONDON, Dec. 28 (CUP).— Diplomatic quarters attributed to a new outbreak of the war of nerves a crop of alarmist rumors which swept across Europe today. They said the rumors were of the sort the Nazis had long been suspected of spreading to confuse and demoralize their opponents. The rumors included those that Hitler was again getting ready to invade Britain, that large forces of Germans were entering Italy, Hungary and Rumania, that Hitler was preparing to over-run unoccupied France and that he was about to strike across Spain to Gibraltar. Hold Rumors Unfounded Usually reliable diplomatic and military informants here had been unable to find any foundation for any of these rumors. They said they suspected that the rumors were spread with the idea of making Great Britain expend its energy in widely separated directions while Hitler completed preparations for a spring campaign.
